The deepseek model successfully audited all text files and found them safe. The PKGBUILD follows standard AUR practices: sources from the project's own GitHub repo, applies a checksummed local patch, uses standard build tools (make, cargo), and has no suspicious network activity or code execution. The LICENSE is a standard ISC license. The only coverage gap is that both models incorrectly skipped the patch file as 'binary' when patch files are text-based diffs that should be reviewed.
data.disagreement_analysis: The qwen model failed to audit the LICENSE file due to an HTTP 400 API error, causing an inconclusive verdict. The deepseek model successfully audited the same file and found it safe. This is a tool failure, not a substantive disagreement about security.
coverage_issues: Both models incorrectly classified 0001-build-linux-allow-skipping-font-install-or-splitting.patch as a binary file and skipped it. Patch files are text-based diffs that should be reviewed for malicious modifications to the build process.
The qwen model experienced an API failure (HTTP 400) when auditing LICENSE, resulting in an incomplete audit.
false_negatives: The patch file 0001-build-linux-allow-skipping-font-install-or-splitting.patch was not reviewed by either model. While it has a valid checksum in the PKGBUILD (mitigating swap risk), the patch content itself should be examined to ensure it doesn't inject malicious build steps or modify source code in harmful ways.
learnings: File type detection should be improved: patch files (.patch, .diff) are text-based and should never be classified as binary. The tool should use file extensions or content inspection (checking for diff headers like '---' and '+++') rather than relying on potentially incorrect metadata.

When an LLM API call fails for a specific file, the audit tool should either retry the request or clearly distinguish between 'file is unsafe' and 'audit incomplete due to tool error' in the final verdict logic.
Patch files applied during build should be prioritized for review even when they have valid checksums, as the checksum only prevents substitution attacks, not malicious content in the original patch.
